answer:
**A feature outage should lead to a defined degraded service, not an accidental model input.** Replacing every missing value with zero can mean something very different from “unknown,” especially if the model never saw that pattern during training. Fallback behavior must be designed and evaluated in advance. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

**Use a tiered response.** Give online feature calls bounded timeouts. Use a sufficiently fresh cached value when its contract permits it. Otherwise use trained missing-value handling, a reduced-feature model, or a deterministic baseline. For high-impact decisions, route uncertain cases to a review or conservative policy appropriate to the actual cost tradeoff.

A circuit breaker can stop repeated calls to a failing dependency and prevent request pileups. Retries need budgets and jitter; retrying every request aggressively can amplify the outage. Expose freshness and fallback mode in logs so degraded predictions are distinguishable from normal ones.

**Test the business behavior.** Simulate total outage, slow responses, partial fields, and stale values. Measure quality, latency, and downstream consequences under each fallback. A service returning HTTP 200 with nonsensical scores is not gracefully degraded.

Recover gradually and verify feature consistency before restoring full traffic. Monitor fallback frequency and duration as operational signals. The correct policy is domain-specific: “always approve,” “always decline,” or “always use defaults” is not universally safe or useful.

**Technical details and references.**

Give feature retrieval a strict deadline smaller than the total request budget. Use a circuit breaker during sustained failure, bounded retries only when safe, and an explicit fallback hierarchy: recent cached features with age limits, a model trained to handle missing features, then a simple business-safe baseline. [1](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/) [2](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

Never replace missing values with arbitrary zeros unless the model contract defines that meaning. Return or log fallback mode, feature age, and reason so degraded traffic is visible and future training does not confuse it with normal operation. Choose fail-open or fail-closed behavior by the decision's consequences; a recommendation feed and a high-risk authorization decision may differ.

Load-test fallback paths and recovery. Unbounded retries can turn one slow Redis instance into a service-wide overload cascade.
